title: Is Crack the future of small-footprint PC game success?
author: Simon Carless
excerpt: Or are we smoking game name? Also: lots of discovery news & the latest GameDiscoverCo Show.

Is Crack the future of small-footprint PC game success?
Or are we smoking game name? Also: lots of discovery news & the latest GameDiscoverCo Show.
Simon Carless
Nov 11, 2026
[The GameDiscoverCo game discovery newsletter is written by ‘how people find your game’ expert & company founder Simon Carless, and is a regular look at how people discover and buy video games in the 2020s.]
Let’s continue with the good stuff - in this case, the good stuff being ‘more profiles of successful PC games in the year of our Gabe 2026’ , since we’re starting to get the hang of specific titles that are being successful, and why. (We know about ‘ most pre-ordered game in the history of both PlayStation & Xbox stores ’ Grand Theft Auto VI, of course…)
Before we start, the wonderful Fabien Sanglard - who’s published a series of ‘game engine black books’ on Wolfenstein, Doom & more, has looked at how hackers unlocked the other games on the 1996 Quake shareware CD , originally gated via $ and a phone call (!). In the end: “The entire protection mechanism relies on security by obscurity.”
[ NEED THE BEST DATA? You can get a free demo of our GameDiscoverCo Pro company-wide ‘Steam deep dive’ & console data, inc. MCP server, by reaching out today - >110 orgs have it. Or, signing up to GDCo Basic gets extra newsletter and Discord access, plus more .]
Game discovery news: Dreadmoor, Ebbtide, Shrek!
Let’s start things out with various game platform & discovery news, rolling up like this:
GDCo’s latest trending unreleased Steam games by wishlist increases , as of yesterday? Just-debuting creepy fishing adventure Dreadmoor hit #1, giga-zombie survival title Ebbtide is at #2, but #3 is maybe the most surprising - a remaster of the 2024 Shrek 2 game?! (But there's an awful lot of Shrek nostalgia out there.)
Elsewhere, upcoming F2P titles Soulframe (#4) & Deadlock (#5) have good interest, and #6 is new co-op action roguelite Chrono Punk . And Warhammer Survivors (#7) is another title, like Dreadmoor, due for release this week. (Special shout-out to My Ransomware Can't Be This Cute?! at #15 based on name alone.)
PlayStation things: the official PlayStation.com pages for Ghost of Yotei and Until Dawn 2 now include ‘PlayStation Exclusive’ logos ; a new Japan-only PlayStation Portal handheld is launching Dec. 10th and includes internal storage, new for PS Portal. ( ‘Future functionality’ is apparently being teased here.)
A note if you look at Steam bundle discounts a lot: Valve made a change related to UX on multi-game/DLC bundles that also have apps within it on sale to show ‘total discount’. Basically: it no longer shows a wrongly small % off (can be as low as 1% or 2%) in those circumstances. (This is a UX change & the price isn’t changing.)
Here’s some more behind-the-scenes analysis on that hit Drawquarium trailer : notable points? ‘Rethinking pacing’ - the trailer doesn’t hit you over the head with the hook, and has done great. And timing Steam personalized calendar adding to just after Next Fest. (160k+ wishlists say they can’t be too wrong…)
AI things: Roblox Build (AI)-made games hold about 1 in 380,000 of the people playing ; Sulka Haro did a big update of his ‘Steam x AI’ data dump ; Nexus Mods is adding public explanations to ‘AI-assisted’ tags ; World Of Warcraft data analysis & add-ons are getting incredibly AI-pilled : “Today, 10,000 developers are using our API and 1,000 are being abusive.”
Valve is really trying not to collect extra data from Australian users, while hewing to new R18+ game access rules , and its latest fix is: “Steam will automatically consider your account age verified if it is at least nine years old and has had a consistent email address or billing information.” (But it’s looking into more, non-invasive ways.)
Game veteran/ ’very online’ guy George Broussard notes “Random data brokers are contacting Unreal Engine 5 devs and paying a *lot* for source code for LLM training” - mid 6 figures cited. (We’ve heard this too across multiple game engines, with no doubt some ‘bad faith’ flippers mixed into this new tributary of the gold rush.)
‘Games as platforms’ news: wow, Fortnite’s One Piece crossover included “a super-rare item called a Pirate Token … [which] grant the team that finds them basically unfettered access to the game’s item shop” to buy anything they want. (Mm, loot boxen - after a furore, Epic disclosed drop rates , and it’s a 1:137,500 chance.)
Why don’t players like dedicated PC ‘launcher’ apps? Apart from the extra clutter and UI issues, here’s another reason : “a November 3 announcement that the PC launcher of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE showed signs of being compromised by a third party.” Here’s a full run-down - remote-access backdoor & crypto stealing DLLs.
Platform microlinks: Epic Games Launcher is officially coming to Steam Deck ; Xbox Cloud Gaming is getting a phone controller and new direct Wi-Fi connectivity for the Xbox Nano ; the Steam Awards 10th anniversary opens Nov. 23rd for player voting; Xbox Game Pass additions inc. Escape Academy 2, Warhammer Survivors.
OUR SPONSOR: player.gg , The Fastest Growing Player Network
player.gg is the fastest growing player network in games: 200K+ real players, actively looking for their next playtest. List yours and let the right ones sign up where they already hang out.
Every signup lands straight in your FirstLook pipeline , with profiles and playtime ready to go. Bundled free with every FirstLook account. 2,000+ studios already use it, from solo indies to AAA teams.
Eden (our CEO) will demo it himself . GDCo subscribers: 30-day free Pro trial, worth $1,599.
Is Crack the future of smaller PC game success?
So, we’ve been following a witty co-op incremental game called Crack for a few days, now. The premise is simple? “Why is there a giant egg in this lab? Your job is simple: crack it open. Don't ask questions.” Your blobby companions are thrown all kinds of curveballs along the way - multiple shell layers, equipment upgrades, surprises & more.
The title topped out at 8,500 concurrents on Steam, and is just outside the Top 100 on Twitch in the last 30 days, with >1.2 million hours watched (!) & organic shortform video interest. Streamers like CaRtOoNz had popular multi-part series playing the game, and GDCo estimates the game at >250k sold and >$1.5m in gross $ LTD.
In chatting to its creator Rafoli (a GDCo newsletter reader!), we thought this Top 15 Steam ‘new game’ seller in October deserved highlighting as an example of what’s to come. Why so? Let’s explain:
This is essentially* a solo dev project, made in just 9 months: 100% handcoded by Rafoli, who has “shipped multiple games before, although I decided to start under a new name for this particular project”, there was external help on the music & also marketing (via Playmakers.co), but the game was basically made by one person.
It’s designed for finite playtime but strong, entertaining game loop: the $8 game ends when you crack open the egg. But there’s a lot of fun with friends ‘meta’ before you get there - little in-game toys like a basketball hoop & whiteboards, unexpected tasks, and underneath, the ‘work harder to upgrade tools’ game loop.
Crack pushes back against the stereotype that games like this are sloppily made: if you look at Rafoli’s Instagram videos about the making of the game, you’ll see videos on making the shop UI interface that are lovingly handcrafted with an eye for chaos. (There’s no AI use here or even asset packs - I did ask.)
For me, the success of Crack - which may eventually gross $4-$5m - is interesting precisely because it appears to be made by a skilled (if pseudonymous) veteran dev. The reason we feel like it’s the future? It’s a cheaper, “relatively small-scope game, but one where a lot of attention went into making the mechanics very polished” , per Rafoli, who adds: “What looks like overnight success is very often not overnight success.”
On the demand side, it’s becoming increasingly clear that there’s a mass of gamers who want $7-12 ‘scenarios’ to play through on Steam with friends, not $40-$60 ‘all-encompassing life tasks in game form’. These games work particularly well if devs understand and encourage the social interplay that make these scenarios fun/funny…
So absolutely, there’s still validity in making a giant AAA game, or a super-complex strategy title, or a niche single-player game (hi, Horses Of Hoofprint Bay .). But this snack-sized, propulsive co-op/incremental submarket is one of the most dynamic, and we’re still learning about what powers it. (We have player survey results on this soon.)
We do run into near-existential ‘low barrier to entry’ questions here - there are a near-infinite number of solo devs who can devote 9 months to making a game like this. But, given it’s the idea (and the execution!) that worked here, we asked Rafoli how he devised & built out Crack’s scenario. Here’s the takeaways:
The initial idea of the game was based around co-op lab experiments: Rafoli tells us: “I wanted players to run random/weird experiments in a laboratory… I realized it would be much more interesting if you were being asked to run these experiments without actually understanding them or why you needed to do them.”
The impersonal lab atmosphere leads to semi-sinister vibes: inspired by games like The Stanley Parable and TV shows like Severance, Rafoli notes: “Sometimes [Crack’s in-game lab] management is incredibly toxic, and sometimes it tries to create this overly happy, work-life-balanced environment.”
The final massive viral hook is the egg-cracking mystery: people like knowing what’s inside things! So ‘what’s in the egg?’ is the ultimate puzzle. It turns out the final reveal is not really that important in Crack. But the journey to uncover that is the real prize. * dabs eyes * As always, it’s the friends we made along the way…
Is this overly portentous analysis for what is ultimately a goofy game about cracking open an egg with your friends? Kinda. But also - this title didn’t 100% randomly become a hit. It has some things it did very right. And if we can’t get to the bottom of that, what’s the point in doing any success analysis at all?
Anyhow, before we go, some supporting data from GameDiscoverCo Pro. Firstly, ‘top games that Crack owners play on Steam they’re >5x more likely to have tried than the average Steam player’ - and there’s a lot of crew-like games in this list:
This means that 58.6% of Crack players also played Peak, and they’re 6.8x more likely than the average Steam players to do so.
We’re estimating playtime at just under 4 hours median/average, close to ‘normal’ completion time, implying high finishing rates. And it’s fairly diverse regionally, with 28% U.S. owners, followed by Germany, Russian Federation, UK, Canada, Turkey, France, then China.
Oh, and to end, here’s GDCo’s Steam player review sentiment analysis (below) . Please note that the listed weaknesses are a fraction of the overall comments, as can be seen by the lower % of red in the ‘sentiment topics’ section, particularly for price:
GameDisco Show: best way to avoid game clones?
It’s here again - the newest GameDiscover Show , ft. myself (Simon) and Post Games’ Chris Plante talking trends. Reminder: sub to the podcast via Apple Podcasts , Spotify & elsewhere (audio), with a video version on YouTube (above).

title: AI Update Part 1: Steam’s AI flood doesn’t mean it’s game over for indies
author: Ross Burton, PhD
text:
AI Update Part 1: Steam’s AI flood doesn’t mean it’s game over for indies
Share:
Author: Ross Burton, PhD, Head of Product and Data
Category: Data Analysis
Published: 11/11/2026
Updated: 11/11/2026
It has been nearly a year since we published our analysis of the breadth of AI disclosures and how those disclosures impact sales . At the time that analysis went largely unnoticed. But one day, the following summer, we had just arrived back from a holiday in Portugal to find that analysis had been picked up by the likes of PC Gamer and Dualshockers! This was a shock to us and a welcomed “viral” moment for our little company.
The interest that analysis received, the kind comments, and the enquiries from inquisitive and excited indie devs was delightful. Both Jennie and I were still working full-time for other people at that point and to be honest, we couldn’t give it the full attention it deserved. Since then, however, we’ve finally built the Game Oracle platform to a point where it matches our original vision and we’ve taken the plunge and decided to work on Game Oracle and our indie studio full-time for at least the next 6 months.
So, with more time on our hands, we figured it’s finally time to address the analysis again, and oh-boy has a lot happened in the Steam market in the last year!
My face, when thinking about addressing the topic of AI in games again… AI slop, AI clones, AI dread… there’s plenty to feel uneasy about. But I don’t want this analysis to be another doom-and-gloom take on game development and AI’s role in it.
Fundamentally, I’m an optimist. I believe data can help us see reality more objectively, while our perspectives and lived experiences shape what that reality means to us personally. But neither data nor experience can tell us how to respond on their own. That’s where our philosophy comes in: guiding our actions, reminding us what’s within our control, and helping us decide what to do next.
I hope this analysis helps keep you informed and eases some anxieties about the world we live in right now. We’re going to deliver it across three parts:
This article: how much is AI being used right now? How has it changed over the last year? And does the wave of AI releases make being an indie impossible to the point where you should give up and move to the country to be a farmer? (Spoiler: no, please don’t do that)
Part 2: we’ll revisit the causal analysis we released last year and, again, ask the question “How does AI disclosure impact sales?”
Part 3: this is a new question, and one I never imagined I would need to ask (and frankly I am sad I have too), how worried should you be about your game getting cloned by AI? I’ll be using our Steam map and some carefully crafted ML models to identify what exactly is being cloned and what we can do about it.
Yes, there is more AI being used now
Let's start with the obvious. Yes, there are more games being released on Steam and yes, more of them are disclosing that they use AI.
AI disclosure rose from 15.2% of releases in January 2025 to 50.1% in October 2026, and the number of overall releases more than tripled. Enjoying this article? Sign up to our newsletter for monthly market insights and the
latest indie innovations

Email By signing up, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy .
Sign me up
The proportion of releases with an AI disclosure back in January of 2025 was 15%, but now half of all new releases have some form of AI disclosure attached to their store page. In that same period, the number of new releases more than tripled; although that spike in October is likely a result of Next Fest.
You’re probably already thinking, didn’t you say this wouldn’t be a doom-and-gloom article? But please, stick with me! As I said, this is just the data and an objective lay of the land. We’ll get to a more optimistic analysis later on.
How are people using AI?
Before I dive into this next section it goes without saying that we’re assuming people are being honest in their disclosures. Like I said in my original analysis last year, I think this is a fair assumption since Valve makes this a requirement for publishing your game.
Valve has a disproportionate amount of control over whether you can access the PC gaming market at volume, and therefore lying to Valve would be stupid. However, people are irrational, so keep this in mind.
Art is the most commonly disclosed use of AI, with 49% reporting AI use and a further 21% reporting human-edited AI work. Marketing and store-page content comes next, at 23% and 8%, respectively. The chart shown above was created using, haha…AI. Well, let me be kinder to myself. I didn’t just point [insert favorite AI chatbot] at the AI disclosures and ask “how are people using AI?”. No, we used a very conservative methodology to try and avoid misleading statistics. To avoid going off on a tangent, I’ll leave the gritty details for the stats nerds in the "Methodologies" section at the end of this article. For everyone else, just know that we’ve done our best to try and not overstate AI use.
The results are pretty clear, and are not too different from our original analysis; AI is overwhelmingly used for art, marketing, and store page images. However, the proportion of disclosures that include some discussion of “human editing” has increased, as has the proportion of other use cases in disclosures; by “human editing” we mean that the disclosure includes some discussion around how AI generated the original asset and then a human edited the final result.
Let’s have a closer look at how exactly each disclosure type has changed.
Among classified AI disclosures, art remains the most common use, while narrative, localisation, music and code become more common in later cohorts. Human-edited AI art also rises, from under 10% to around 25% of disclosures. The big takeaway from this graph is that art remains the biggest use case, but disclosure around code, localisation, and narrative text/dialogue has increased over this period. The biggest shift is the rise of “human-editing” remarks in the AI disclosure text, especially for art.
Perhaps this is driven by anxiety around how AI art is perceived. People might be hoping that showing a human intervention between the AI generation and the final product will help soften the blow? I’ll leave that up to your interpretation.
Has the wave of AI games saturated the market?
We know there is a wave of AI-generated (or at least partly generated) games flooding the Steam store, but is this making it harder for indie developers to be discovered and to reach their financial goals?
This is not a simple question to answer. First of all, what even is success?
Without getting too deep here, I’m going to use a realistic milestone. I know that most indie developers publishing on Steam are releasing their first commercial game and in my (I will argue, informed) opinion, an objective of 1000 sales is both a healthy and realistic target for success. If you want further justification for this I point you to our previous analysis on indie success and longevity on Steam .
So with that in mind, let us reframe the quest to "As Steam releases have surged, have the number of games reaching 1,000 sales stayed fixed, or grown with the Steam releases?"
To answer this question, we took every monthly release cohort from January 2025 to September 2026 in which all games are at least 30 days old (that is 21 months and 36,228 Steam releases) and we fitted a log-log regression model on the number of games with at least 1,000 estimated sales against releases that month.
The slope of this model (shown in the graph below) shows whether games selling 1000 copies stay fixed or scale with the volume of releases. The most recent months had the most releases, yet still produced more games reaching 1,000 sales despite having less time to get there. Overall, this suggests that the number of games finding an audience is growing, not staying fixed.
More releases have brought more successes, but each game's odds of selling 1,000 copies have still slipped a little, from roughly 1 in 5 to 1 in 6, and some of that slip is just because the newest games haven't had as long to sell.
We also compared the first three months of 2025 with the latest three and re-checked the results several ways.
As releases roughly doubled, the number of games reaching 1,000 sales rose from 763 to 1,311, but the proportion reaching 1,000 sales fell from about 20% to 16.5%. Part of that drop is because newer games have had less time to sell: counting only games at least six months old, the gap narrows to about 19.6% vs 18%.

In conclusion, keep your chin up!
There’s plenty here to feel uneasy about, but I’m leaving this analysis more hopeful than when I started.

My takeaway is to keep our ambitions grounded, stay curious about the market, and put our energy into the things we can influence: what we make, who we make it for, and how we help those people find it.

Methodology (for the nerds)
A quick look under the hood of where these numbers come from, how we sorted AI disclosures into categories, and how we checked the "the market is not saturated" claim.
The Data

Used AI: the disclosure says AI was used here.
Used AI, but human-edited: it says a person reworked the AI output. Saying someone “reviewed”, “selected” or “directed” the output wasn’t enough for this label.
Not disclosed: the disclosure doesn’t say AI was used here. This doesn’t mean the game didn’t use AI for that category. It only means the statement doesn’t say so.

How the labels were made
We labelled a sample of 1,000 disclosures, with an AI model doing the first pass. I then checked 100 of them by hand, and then we audited the whole set against a few house rules so that similar cases were labelled the same way. For example:
Art made only for the store page counts as marketing, not game art.
“We used AI for audio” with no detail counts as music, voice and sound effects.

How well does it work?
We kept the 100 hand-checked disclosures out of training and tested on them:
It picked the right label for a category 96% of the time, against about 79% for a lazy baseline that always guesses the most common label.
It got all nine categories right on 73% of disclosures.
It’s weaker on some things. It caught only 4 of the 9 text/dialogue uses in the test set, and the test set had no live-generated examples at all, so treat the live-generation numbers as rough.

Is the market saturated?
The worry goes like this: AI makes games cheaper to make, more games come out, and a fixed number of players gets split across more and more titles. If that’s true, the number of games that do well each month should stay roughly flat however many come out, and each game’s chances should shrink.

β = 0 would mean a fixed number of hits each month, whatever the number of releases. That’s the “fixed pie” world and the worst case scenario.
β = 1 would mean hits grow in step with releases, so each game’s odds stay the same.
Anywhere in between means more releases bring more hits, but each game’s odds go down.

More releases came with more hits; there were 763 in the first three months against 1,311 in the last three months. The share of games that became hits did fall, from about 20% to 16.5%, but after the volume adjustment it’s roughly flat, at about 20% at both ends.

Defining hits with the low and high sales estimates instead of the central one barely moved β (0.72 and 0.74).

We didn’t compare AI and non-AI games here, and this isn’t a causal analysis. It also can’t tell you whether developers are making more money, because 1,000 units is a milestone, not revenue. AI Update Part 1: Steam’s AI flood doesn’t mean it’s game over for indies

Author: Ross Burton, PhD, Head of Product and Data
Category: Data Analysis
Published: 11/11/2026
Updated: 11/11/2026

It has been nearly a year since we published our analysis of the breadth of AI disclosures and how those disclosures impact sales. At the time that analysis went largely unnoticed. But one day, the following summer, we had just arrived back from a holiday in Portugal to find that analysis had been picked up by the likes of PC Gamer and Dualshockers! This was a shock to us and a welcomed “viral” moment for our little company.

The interest that analysis received, the kind comments, and the enquiries from inquisitive and excited indie devs was delightful. Both Jennie and I were still working full-time for other people at that point and to be honest, we couldn’t give it the full attention it deserved. Since then, however, we’ve finally built the Game Oracle platform to a point where it matches our original vision and we’ve taken the plunge and decided to work on Game Oracle and our indie studio full-time for at least the next 6 months.

So, with more time on our hands, we figured it’s finally time to address the analysis again, and oh-boy has a lot happened in the Steam market in the last year!

 

AI slop, AI clones, AI dread… there’s plenty to feel uneasy about. But I don’t want this analysis to be another doom-and-gloom take on game development and AI’s role in it.

Fundamentally, I’m an optimist. I believe data can help us see reality more objectively, while our perspectives and lived experiences shape what that reality means to us personally. But neither data nor experience can tell us how to respond on their own. That’s where our philosophy comes in: guiding our actions, reminding us what’s within our control, and helping us decide what to do next.

I hope this analysis helps keep you informed and eases some anxieties about the world we live in right now. We’re going to deliver it across three parts:

  1. This article: how much is AI being used right now? How has it changed over the last year? And does the wave of AI releases make being an indie impossible to the point where you should give up and move to the country to be a farmer? (Spoiler: no, please don’t do that)

  2. Part 2: we’ll revisit the causal analysis we released last year and, again, ask the question “How does AI disclosure impact sales?”

  3. Part 3: this is a new question, and one I never imagined I would need to ask (and frankly I am sad I have too), how worried should you be about your game getting cloned by AI? I’ll be using our Steam map and some carefully crafted ML models to identify what exactly is being cloned and what we can do about it.

Yes, there is more AI being used now

Let's start with the obvious. Yes, there are more games being released on Steam and yes, more of them are disclosing that they use AI.

The proportion of releases with an AI disclosure back in January of 2025 was 15%, but now half of all new releases have some form of AI disclosure attached to their store page. You’re probably already thinking, didn’t you say this wouldn’t be a doom-and-gloom article? But please, stick with me! As I said, this is just the data and an objective lay of the land. We’ll get to a more optimistic analysis later on.

How are people using AI?

Before I dive into this next section it goes without saying that we’re assuming people are being honest in their disclosures. Like I said in my original analysis last year, I think this is a fair assumption since Valve makes this a requirement for publishing your game. 

Valve has a disproportionate amount of control over whether you can access the PC gaming market at volume, and therefore lying to Valve would be stupid. However, people are irrational, so keep this in mind.

 

The chart shown above was created using, haha…AI. Well, let me be kinder to myself. I didn’t just point [insert favorite AI chatbot] at the AI disclosures and ask “how are people using AI?”. No, we used a very conservative methodology to try and avoid misleading statistics. To avoid going off on a tangent, I’ll leave the gritty details for the stats nerds in the "Methodologies" section at the end of this article. For everyone else, just know that we’ve done our best to try and not overstate AI use.

The results are pretty clear, and are not too different from our original analysis; AI is overwhelmingly used for art, marketing, and store page images. Let’s have a closer look at how exactly each disclosure type has changed.

 

The big takeaway from this graph is that art remains the biggest use case, but disclosure around code, localisation, and narrative text/dialogue has increased over this period. The biggest shift is the rise of “human-editing” remarks in the AI disclosure text, especially for art.

Perhaps this is driven by anxiety around how AI art is perceived. People might be hoping that showing a human intervention between the AI generation and the final product will help soften the blow? I’ll leave that up to your interpretation.

We know there is a wave of AI-generated (or at least partly generated) games flooding the Steam store, but is this making it harder for indie developers to be discovered and to reach their financial goals?

This is not a simple question to answer. First of all, what even is success? 

Without getting too deep here, I’m going to use a realistic milestone. I know that most indie developers publishing on Steam are releasing their first commercial game and in my (I will argue, informed) opinion, an objective of 1000 sales is both a healthy and realistic target for success. If you want further justification for this I point you to our previous analysis on indie success and longevity on Steam.

There’s still room to make something worth playing, and that’s a future I’m excited to be part of. See you in part 2!
